sources.title: National Park Service: Mogollon in the American Southwest
sources.note: Direct regional description and broad circa 200 to 1450 archaeological chronology. Population contributions to later communities are probable, not an exact assignment of all descendants.

sources.title: National Park Service: Jornada Mogollon
sources.note: Direct first paragraphs and Lake Lucero/Huntington discussion. Regional construction and subsistence, water and possible gypsum plaster; no claim that all Mogollon branches used the same practices.

sources.title: National Park Service: the Tularosa Mogollon at Gila
sources.note: Direct 2024 article: lack of written language, excavated yucca sandals, shelter/resources and preserved maize cobs. More recent circa 1270s to early 1300s occupation preferred to older NPS 1270 to 1290 account. No recovered shampoo residue claimed.

sources.title: National Park Service: Cave 1 and the family home
sources.note: Direct site interpretation: small storage rooms, likely enclosed living space and cooking hearth; 32 plant species, 24 wild.

sources.title: National Park Service: dating Gila’s Cave 3
sources.note: Direct original beams, sampled plug, mostly 1280s rooms and much earlier cave use. Draft preserves distinction between timber cut date and construction.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Bowl with Two Rabbits
sources.note: Original museum catalogue, object 1978.412.118; mid-ninth to twelfth century, Mimbres/New Mexico, rabbit motif and food animal. Specific object distinguished from written language.

sources.title: Western New Mexico University Museum: permanent exhibitions
sources.note: Direct/indexed museum description includes miniature vessels and vessels made by children alongside Mimbres ceramic sequences. No specific maker, age or toy function invented.

sources.title: Navajo Nation: history and homeland
sources.note: Introduction identifies Diné Bikéyah as Navajoland in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. Only identity used; page retains obsolete council totals and those are not copied.

sources.title: Bureau of Land Management: Defensive Sites of Dinétah
sources.note: Direct description: seventeenth/eighteenth-century Navajo pueblitos, defensive positions, shelter and cooking, roofs, hooded fireplaces, hogan foundations and doorway peepholes.

sources.title: National Park Service: New Mexico fiber arts traditions
sources.note: Diné upright looms, adoption of churra sheep and wool. Broader thirteenth-century Southwest cotton textiles are not assigned specifically to Navajo people.

sources.title: Hubbell Trading Post: sheep and trade
sources.note: Where Are the Sheep? Trading post established in 1878, exchanged products/supplies, community services and Ganado Red design. Trader’s promotional claim of shared prosperity not adopted.

sources.title: Hubbell Trading Post: Sheep, Wool and Weaving
sources.note: Archived announcement explicitly dates workshop July 10, 2016, despite later page-update date. Workshops began in 2000; dyeing, spinning and weaving.

sources.title: Navajo Nation: Treaty of 1868 anniversary leadership messages
sources.note: Direct access intermittent; indexed original statement by Speaker Lorenzo Bates for the 2018 anniversary confirms forced removal in 1864, four-year imprisonment and negotiated return.

sources.title: Navajo Nation courts: Treaty of 1868
sources.note: Primary treaty text concluded June 1, 1868. Article XII promises purchase of 15,000 sheep and goats and return transport/provisions. Promises not represented as evidence of complete delivery.

sources.title: Navajo Nation Council: Our Legacy and History
sources.note: Official institutional history: 1923 council and 1989 separation of powers. No current officeholder or obsolete membership count repeated.

sources.title: Navajo government development: institutional history
sources.note: Official December 1989 Resolution CD-68-89 separation of Chairman and Vice-Chairman into Executive Branch, President and Vice-President.

sources.title: National Archives: Navajo enlistment and development of the code
sources.note: Original archival educational account: 29 recruits on May 5, 1942; code initially 211 terms and alphabet, rather than merely speaking ordinary Navajo.

sources.title: National Endowment for the Humanities: Saying Hello in Navajo
sources.note: Summer 2022 interview with Navajo scholar Shelly C. Lowe. Exact greeting yá’át’ééh translated It is good; matrilineal clan introduction; personal Ganado school memories. Modern written witness, not an early inscription.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Missing and collision-checked. Indexed 800 to 1000, decoded world-800 polygon bbox -112.8917 to -96.6016, 20.6702 to 30.4415 lies chiefly far south of the Southwestern Mogollon heartland. Public opening states displacement explicitly; no geometry repair claimed. Narrative distinguishes Jornada, Mimbres and Tularosa examples instead of manufacturing a centralized state. Modern archaeological name not ancient self-name. Gila 1270s/early 1300s material deliberately later than coverage interval; no inference of disappearance from settlement relocation. No modern nation aliases absorbed.

All three missing and collision-checked. Navajo Nation introduction explicitly identifies Diné Bikéyah as Navajoland; Navaho is a historical spelling also attested by Smithsonian treaty facsimile title Treaty with the Navaho, 1868 (https://americanindian.si.edu/nationtonation/pdf/Navajo-Treaty-1868.pdf). Decoded first outlines all lie in the Southwest but differ: navajo 1500 to 1530 bbox -109.7237 to -103.0024, 32.2396 to 37.3433; navaho 1530 to 1650 bbox -111.1853 to -104.6332, 33.8492 to 37.3354; dine-bikeyah 1492 to 1500 bbox -111.8873 to -107.0021, 34.2116 to 37.8903. Sharing is explicitly through the same people/homeland history, not an assertion of identical borders or consecutive sovereign states. Contemporary Navajo Nation continuity is clear; no other Native nations absorbed.
